tldr: Researchers developed and demonstrated "X-Nav," a system enabling a bipedal humanoid to autonomously navigate roughly 100 meters from an indoor lobby to an outdoor store in an adjacent building without prior maps, using only monocular camera video and natural language instructions.
hero_caption: Overview of X-Navarch, the agentic workflow comprising the overall X-Nav architecture. It integrates a planner that decomposes instructions, the path-following model MELIOR-N, the goal approach skill MELIOR-X, and a low-level control layer that compensates for latency and avoids obstacles on the real robot.
overview:
For humanoid robots to perform practical work in society, they must first be able to navigate to instructed destinations autonomously. However, no matter how high models score on visual-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks in simulation, they often fail when deployed on real hardware due to a severe "sim-to-real" gap. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on 10 to 15-meter indoor scanned environments, ignoring the heavy camera shake caused by walking, drastic indoor-to-outdoor visual transitions, and dynamic pedestrians and vehicles.

To address this, the authors built "X-Nav," an integrated navigation framework designed to bridge three core gaps: task specification, training data, and real-robot deployment. They developed a three-tier data engine combining large-scale synthetic data from open-source scenes, a digital twin constructed from a real-world site scan, and real-robot movement logs. For navigation models, they introduced two variants taking only onboard monocular RGB images: MELIOR-A, which outputs low-level actions, and MELIOR-N, which outputs goal coordinates in image space. In addition, they designed "X-Navarch," an agentic workflow that pairs a planner for decomposing natural language instructions, MELIOR-X for high-precision final approaches from several meters away, and latency compensation with obstacle avoidance layers.

In real-world experiments using the bipedal humanoid "Lingxi X2," the robot successfully navigated 96.6 meters from a building lobby through automatic doors, along outdoor roads, to the front of a convenience store in an adjacent building. It flexibly handled mid-course instruction updates, crossing pedestrians, and vehicles, marking the first demonstration of autonomous indoor-to-outdoor bipedal navigation across sites without prior environmental maps.
contributions: Demonstrated the first real-world, long-horizon (~100 m) autonomous indoor-to-outdoor navigation on a bipedal humanoid guided solely by natural language instructions without prior maps.
Constructed a three-tier data engine combining open-source scenes, an on-site digital twin, and real-robot logs capable of collecting recovery data from failures via DAgger.

Developed MELIOR, a visual-language navigation foundation model inferring actions or goal coordinates directly from monocular RGB images, alongside MELIOR-X, an explicit tracking skill for precise near-goal approach.

Proposed X-Navarch, an agentic workflow that breaks down high-level human instructions into subtasks, compensates for image and inference latency using LiDAR and odometry, and avoids dynamic obstacles during locomotion.

sections.heading: Bridging the Three Gaps Where Simulation Benchmarks Fail on Real Hardware
sections.summary: While recent VLN benchmarks have advanced rapidly, they fall short of long-horizon navigation on real humanoids. Sim-to-real discrepancies stem from three areas—task formulation, training data, and deployment implementation—all of which X-Nav is designed to solve comprehensively.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to perform autonomous tasks in workplaces, they must first reach their destinations on foot. Visual-Language Navigation (VLN), which generates movements from language commands and camera images, has been widely studied. With simulation benchmarks like R2R-CE and RxR-CE seeing success rates surpass 70%, the field seemed to approach its "GPT moment." Yet executing long-horizon navigation on real hardware remains difficult. The authors attribute this to three distinct gaps:

- Task Formulation Gap: Benchmarks center on static 10–15 m indoor scans, considering a stop within 3 m a success. Real-world tasks span nearly 100 m, demanding tolerance to gait-induced camera shake, drastic indoor-to-outdoor lighting and field-of-view shifts, moving cars and pedestrians, and precise stopping at entrance thresholds.
- Data Gap: Static indoor scan datasets lack the visual appearance of actual deployment sites and completely omit the walking sway and stopping dynamics of physical robots. Simply scaling up synthetic data is insufficient; site- and robot-specific data are crucial.
- Deployment Gap: A trained model alone cannot operate a robot. An end-to-end framework requires surrounding modules to parse abstract user commands, correct goal drift caused by inference latency while walking, and actively avoid dynamic obstacles.

To close all three gaps, the authors developed X-Nav, integrating a multi-tier data engine, the MELIOR navigation models, and the X-Navarch deployment workflow.

sections.heading: System Overview: Three Nested Loops and Two Navigation Paradigms
sections.summary: X-Nav consists of three components: a data engine, the MELIOR navigation model family, and the X-Navarch agentic workflow. These operate as three nested feedback loops ranging from high-frequency locomotion to site adaptation.
sections.details:
### Three Nested Loops
The X-Nav architecture is structured into three feedback loops operating at different time scales:

- Innermost Layer (Locomotion Control Loop): MELIOR infers actions or waypoints from the robot's onboard monocular RGB camera, sending commands to the walking controller through an obstacle avoidance layer.
- Intermediate Layer (Subtask Management Loop): A planner breaks down instructions into subtasks, routing execution to coarse path-following (MELIOR) or object targeting (MELIOR-X) while monitoring success.
- Outermost Layer (Site Adaptation Loop): Deployment sites are scanned to build digital twins for simulation-based fine-tuning and evaluation prior to real-world deployment. Execution logs from the robot are fed back into the data pipeline.

### Implicit Path Following vs. Explicit Goal Approach
To accomplish long-horizon tasks, navigation is split into two phases: path following and goal approach. Long-distance traversal across dozens of meters is handled by implicit navigation (MELIOR), where policy behavior is internalized within model weights to adapt to diverse visual landmarks and language descriptions. Conversely, the final approach to within meters of a target (e.g., a vending machine or store entrance) is governed by explicit navigation (MELIOR-X), which tracks target masks and relative coordinates in real time.

### Robot Platform and Hardware
Experiments were conducted on the Lingxi X2 bipedal humanoid. The primary navigation model relies strictly on the head-mounted monocular RGB camera (640×480, 79° horizontal FOV) without external camera rigs. Onboard LiDAR and leg odometry are used exclusively for goal depth registration, low-level gait stability, and reactive obstacle avoidance.

sections.heading: Data Engine: From Large-Scale Synthetic Scenes to Real Robot Logs
sections.summary: To ensure reliable deployment, the authors combined three complementary data streams: diverse open-source synthetic environments, site-specific digital twins, and real-robot motion logs capturing gait sway and physical dynamics.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Simulator Design and Trajectory Generation
The authors built "X-Nav-Sim" on Isaac Sim. Occupancy grids are generated from scene geometry, and $A^*$ plans paths with safety margins (0.35 m clearance). To prevent directional bias for a given target, multiple goal poses (G1–G4) are sampled around the object and pre-checked for visibility and occlusion. A VLM then automatically writes natural language instructions based on keyframes and map data collected during trajectory replays.

### 3.3.1 Large-Scale Open-Source Scenes (X-Nav-Syn)
To provide broad spatial and semantic variety, 1,095 scenes were assembled from datasets such as VLNVerse and SAGE-3D, generating 1.11 million steps. Combined with replayed trajectories from R2R, RxR, and SRDF, the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pool reached approximately 6.31 million navigation samples.

### 3.3.2 Digital Twin Collection (X-Nav-Twin)
The actual deployment venue (an office lobby) was captured with a handheld scanner. A digital twin was generated using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for visual fidelity and mesh geometry for collision checks. Crucially, "Correction Windows" were collected here: the model navigated autonomously within the twin, and expert recovery actions and stopping decisions were recorded using DAgger upon deviations. In a 500-trajectory set, roughly 15,000 of the 48,000 total windows were recovery samples.

### 3.3.3 Real-Robot Logs (X-Nav-Real) and Training Mix
RGB feeds and kinematic logs were recorded directly on the Lingxi X2 to capture physical gait wobble and drift. The final MELIOR-N training mixture contains ~8.55 million samples: 6.31 million navigation examples (73.8%) blended with 2.24 million general vision-spatial samples (26.2%) from sources like LLaVA-Video and VSI-590K.

sections.heading: The MELIOR Navigation Models: Action Prediction and Visual Waypointing
sections.summary: MELIOR is an autoregressive VLM that infers navigation decisions from current and past monocular RGB frames. It supports two modes under a unified input structure: MELIOR-A for low-level actions and MELIOR-N for goal coordinates.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 MELIOR-A (Action-Based)
MELIOR-A takes a text prompt and up to 8 recent RGB frames to predict a sequence of up to 4 primitive actions per step (forward 0.25 m, turn 15°, stop). This output space matches standard simulation benchmarks. On the real robot, the 4-step sequence is aggregated into a single relative displacement command, enabling smooth forward movement of up to ~1 m per inference cycle.

### 4.3 MELIOR-N (Goal-Based)
MELIOR-N predicts target locations using four special mode tokens:

- `<visible>`: When the next waypoint is visible, it outputs pixel coordinates $(u, v)$, distance $r$, azimuth $\phi$, and target heading $\psi$.
- `<polar>`: When the target lies beyond the field of view or behind obstacles, it outputs relative distance and orientation $(r, \phi, \psi)$ in the robot's local frame.
- `<rotate>`: Outputs an in-place rotation angle $\psi$.
- `<stop>`: Issued when the instruction criteria are fulfilled.

Numerical coordinates are quantized across 365 dedicated vocabulary tokens. Distance bins are spaced logarithmically to maintain fine resolution close to the robot.

### 4.4 Two-Stage Training Pipeline
Both variants undergo supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the large-scale synthetic navigation and visual QA corpora, followed by DAgger-style fine-tuning in simulation. Providing expert corrections when the policy veers off course teaches the models to autonomously recover from navigation drift during deployment.

sections.heading: MELIOR-X: High-Precision Explicit Approach for the Final Meters
sections.summary: While end-to-end models can guide a robot to a target area, precise positioning in front of doors or vending machines remains challenging. MELIOR-X combines open-vocabulary detection, SAM3 mask tracking, and LiDAR depth to execute metric approaches.
sections.details:
### Attribute-Aware Target Acquisition and Verification
Upon receiving a query (e.g., "blue sofa"), the LocateAnything-3B open-vocabulary detector proposes candidate regions. A lightweight VLM verifier (based on Qwen3-VL-2B) then validates these candidates against category, color, appearance, and structural descriptions. To prevent false positives, a candidate must pass verification across two consecutive frames before being confirmed as the active target.

### Fast Mask Propagation with SAM3
Once confirmed, the target is stored in the visual memory of SAM3 (Segment Anything Model 3). Subsequent tracking runs purely via mask propagation at 20 Hz without calling the VLM. Restricting language reasoning to target initialization and re-detection achieves high tracking speed alongside perceptual robustness.

### Mask-LiDAR Fusion and Approach Control
Calibrated LiDAR points are projected into the detected image mask $M_t$. By filtering points within an eroded center box and isolating the foreground cluster from depth histograms, the system extracts the median 3D position $\mathbf{p}^B_t$ (distance $d_t$, bearing $\theta_t$) relative to the robot. If the target drops near the bottom of the frame, tracking automatically handoffs to an onboard downward-angled RGB-D camera.

An approach controller applies proportional control to distance and bearing errors, prioritizing in-place turns over forward velocity when bearing deviation is high. The robot halts safely upon reaching a preset standoff distance from the target.

sections.heading: X-Navarch: Agentic Workflow for Latency Compensation and Obstacle Avoidance
sections.summary: X-Navarch handles high-level subtask decomposition, corrects for walking-induced inference delays via a goal adapter, and relies on a three-tier avoidance mechanism to ensure robust real-world execution on humanoids.
sections.details:
### Planner and Subtask Management
Human requests (e.g., "buy water from the vending machine") are often abstract. A multimodal planner built on NavGPT-3 inspects forward-facing RGB frames and generates concise one-sentence subtasks, such as "exit through the door and turn right" or "locate the store," dispatching them to MELIOR-N (waypoint tracking) or MELIOR-X (object targeting). The planner reviews progress upon subtask completion to advance to the next step or initiate recovery.

### Goal Adapter for Latency Compensation
On physical hardware, the robot continues walking while camera images are sent and processed by the inference model. To prevent target drift caused by this latency, a goal adapter tracks the goal point. A 2D pixel goal from image timestamp $t_0$ is unprojected into a 3D coordinate via LiDAR depth and anchored to the robot's local odometry frame. Once inference returns at timestamp $t_1$, this anchored 3D point is re-expressed relative to the robot's current position, preserving spatial accuracy despite network and computation lag.

### Three-Layer Obstacle Avoidance
Operating without a pre-built map, X-Navarch addresses obstacles at three distinct levels:

- Planner Layer: Identifies macroscopic obstacles in front-facing images and inserts instructions such as "walk to the left of the traffic cone."
- Model Layer: MELIOR-N is trained with obstacle margins, naturally placing pixel waypoints on free ground surfaces.
- Hardware Local Layer: A real-time local planner sits between navigation waypoints and the walking controller, using live LiDAR range data to dynamically circumnavigate static obstacles or halt for crossing pedestrians and vehicles.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 96.6-Meter Real-World Traversal and Digital Twin Adaptation
sections.summary: Lingxi X2 completed an autonomous 96.6 m walk from an indoor lobby to an outdoor store, handling mid-run goal revisions, vehicles, and pedestrians. Training on digital twin recovery data doubled indoor lobby success rates from 40% to 80%.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Long-Horizon Real-World Deployment on Lingxi X2
The robot tackled an indoor-to-outdoor mission starting in an office lobby, passing through glass doors, walking down outdoor streets, and halting at the entrance of a convenience store (Lawson) in an adjacent building. No prior map or pre-recorded paths were provided.

- MELIOR-A Run: Completed the 96.6 m route (34.2 m indoors, 62.4 m outdoors) in 3 minutes and 24 seconds. At 9.1 m, an operator revised the command to "go to the store in the next building"; the robot rotated on the spot and re-oriented its path. Passing through glass doors at 34.2 m presented a stark transition into bright outdoor sunlight, yet the model maintained its trajectory. At roughly 64 m, the robot autonomously stopped for 24 seconds to yield to a crossing car and pedestrians, before finishing accurately at the 96.6 m mark.
- X-Navarch + MELIOR-N Run: Starting from higher-level commands, the planner dynamically structured subtasks along a route containing 3 dynamic obstacles, 2 static obstacles, and 2 narrow passages. The system negotiated traffic cones and executed local avoidance around carts and cleaning robots to reach the goal.

### 7.2 Sim-to-Real Adaptation via Digital Twin
Evaluated over 100 episodes in the lobby digital twin, a baseline model fine-tuned only on reference trajectories achieved a 40% success rate within 3 m (SR@3m) with 52 continuous wall collisions. Adding DAgger-based recovery and stopping windows improved SR@3m to 80% (and STOP-SR@3m to 78%), while collisions plummeted to 3. Deploying this adapted policy to the physical Lingxi X2 ensured smooth traversal in the actual lobby.

### 7.3 Standard Benchmark Performance
On R2R-CE (val-unseen), MELIOR-N set the top score among monocular RGB models, achieving a 70.5% success rate and 65.1% SPL. MELIOR-A reached a 66.1% success rate, confirming strong performance without requiring panoramic views or external mapping tools.

sections.heading: Related Work: Enabling Real Humanoid Locomotion with Monocular RGB and Agents
sections.summary: VLN research has evolved from discrete graphs to continuous domains and large multimodal models. While legged robots have begun adopting VLN, X-Nav advances the field by covering nearly 100 m across indoor and outdoor spaces using only monocular RGB and agentic control.
sections.details:
### Visual-and-Language Navigation (VLN) Trends
VLN has shifted from graph-based navigation in simulators like Habitat to continuous environments. Recent systems, such as Qwen-RobotNav (15.6M samples) and Robostral Navigate, build on video-capable VLMs trained at scale. While action spaces vary widely—ranging from discrete steps to metric waypoints and image pixels—MELIOR unifies discrete action output (MELIOR-A) and multimodal spatial targets (MELIOR-N) within a single monocular RGB framework.

### Legged and Humanoid Robot Navigation
Recent studies like NaVILA, DualVLN, and TANGO have evaluated quadrupedal or small humanoid platforms (such as the Unitree G1), but their real-world trials were limited to single-domain settings (indoor-only or outdoor-only) spanning tens of meters. Broader navigation systems typically relied on pre-scanned spatial memory or external mapping engines. X-Nav requires no prior global maps, operating strictly on onboard RGB frames and text instructions across an indoor-to-outdoor site.

### Agentic Workflows and Open-Vocabulary Tracking
Applying LLMs for high-level planning (e.g., NavGPT variants) and foundation models like SAM for tracking has gained significant traction. X-Navarch tailors these techniques to the dynamics of bipedal walking, integrating latency correction and real-time obstacle avoidance to ensure robust operation in dynamic physical spaces.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Toward Humanoids Walking to Work on Their Own
sections.summary: X-Nav demonstrates autonomous long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor navigation on a bipedal humanoid. Combining a multi-tier data engine, MELIOR, and X-Navarch provides practical principles for overcoming long-standing sim-to-real gaps.
sections.details:
This work introduced X-Nav, enabling the Lingxi X2 bipedal humanoid to autonomously execute ~100 m indoor-to-outdoor navigation guided solely by natural language instructions. This performance is backed by a data engine combining synthetic environments, digital twin correction windows, and real-robot logs; the monocular RGB-based MELIOR model; and the latency- and obstacle-aware X-Navarch agentic workflow. Digital twin adaptation was shown to double model success rates prior to physical deployment.

Future research directions include navigating multi-floor environments using stairs and elevators, manipulating door handles, and building persistent, long-term spatial memory (such as scene graphs) that accumulates and updates environmental knowledge over repeated journeys.

sections.heading: Appendix: Token Design, System Parameters, and Future Local Policies
sections.summary: The appendix details the token scheme and simulation decoding rules for MELIOR-N, hardware deployment parameters, and architectural plans for a learned local obstacle-avoidance policy.
sections.details:
### Appendix A: MELIOR-N Token Design and Decoding
MELIOR-N uses an expanded vocabulary of 365 dedicated tokens. Autoregressive decoding outputs a mode token (`<visible>`, `<polar>`, `<rotate>`, `<stop>`), followed by mode-specific coordinate, range, and angle tokens, ending with `<end>`. Distance $r$ is binned logarithmically to allocate higher precision near the robot. In simulation, `<visible>` pixel predictions are back-projected via depth maps into 3D points, which are converted into up to 4 discrete navigation primitives along the mesh's shortest path.

### Appendices B & C: Hardware Configuration and Evaluation
On the physical Lingxi X2, MELIOR-N's target locations are anchored to the local odometry frame, with new inference passes initiated roughly every 4 seconds. For MELIOR-X, LiDAR point projection uses an eroded 2D bounding box to discard edge noise, followed by percentile filtering to isolate foreground clusters.

### Appendix D: Outlook for a Learned Local Policy
While X-Navarch currently relies on a geometric local planner for obstacle avoidance, future revisions aim to substitute this with a learned local navigation policy. Such a policy would take target coordinates, scene embeddings, and robot state to drive walking controllers directly. Decoupling robot-specific encoders could allow seamless transfer to quadrupeds or other humanoid platforms.

takeaways: Monocular RGB images alone are sufficient for long-horizon outdoor navigation without prior maps when paired with proper tokenization (visible pixels + out-of-view polar coordinates) and large-scale training.
The key to sim-to-real transfer is not raw data scale, but "Correction Windows": training on recovery actions within a site-specific digital twin doubled success rates from 40% to 80%.
Real-world robot deployment demands practical system-level integration, such as a Goal Adapter that rewinds odometry to compensate for elapsed inference time while the robot is moving.
Decoupling coarse path-following over dozens of meters (implicit VLM) from final approach within meters of an object (explicit SAM3 + LiDAR tracking) creates an effective, robust architecture.
limitations: Evaluations were restricted to flat single-floor surfaces without vertical traversal, excluding stair climbing, elevator use, or interacting with doors that require turning door handles.
Site-specific digital twin fine-tuning was tested only within a single office lobby, leaving adaptation costs and scalability across diverse real-world environments unverified.
The system lacks persistent long-term spatial memory (such as permanent scene graphs), preventing it from improving efficiency or refining environmental understanding over multiple runs.
